text: model: 2PL model 31 items fits closely (RMSEA = 0.016, CFI = 0.987). decision: raw cut score 18 classifies candidates estimated accuracy 0.86 consistency 0.81 (kappa = 0.61). title: Case study: A certification exam, from field test to pass/fail
text: whole analysis 40 lines R. Every function returns pipeline, record builds go. full pipeline walk-runs exam every stage, including assembling parallel forms monitoring item bank exam goes live.
code: library(mirtverse)  p <- mv_pipeline("Certification exam: Form A field test") p <- set_blueprint(p, c(Ethics = 4, Practice = 5, Law = 3),                    construct = "Professional knowledge for certification",                    use = "pass/fail certification", reliability = 0.85) p <- design_field_test(p, n_forms = 2, n_per_form = 600, items = 32,                        reps = 2, seed = 1) p <- acknowledge(p, check = "recovery", note = "Sample fixed by the testing window")  p <- add_responses(p, certexam, items = 3:34, key = certexam_key,                    id = "id", group = "language") flags(p)                                  # Q14: possible miskey (block) p <- drop_items(p, "Q14", note = "Key confirmed wrong by the item writer")  p <- calibrate(p, model = "2PL") flags(p, stage = "calibration")           # DIF, local dependence, reliability p <- override(p, check = "dif_large",               note = "Translation reviewed; French version revised") p <- acknowledge(p, check = "dif_moderate", note = "Sent to the bias panel") p <- acknowledge(p, check = "local_dependence",                  note = "Q21 and Q22 share a case; keep them apart on forms") p <- acknowledge(p, check = "low_reliability",                  note = "Operational forms will be longer than the field test")  p <- bank_items(p, name = "Certification bank") p <- set_cuts(p, cuts = 18, scale = "raw", labels = c("Fail", "Pass")) p$cuts$summary                            # accuracy, consistency, kappa p <- score_persons(p) p <- acknowledge(p, check = "cut_precision",                  note = "Add items near the cut to the operational forms") p <- acknowledge(p, check = "score_reliability",                  note = "Field-test scores are not reported to candidates") p <- check_security(p, leaked = c("Q01", "Q02", "Q03", "Q04", "Q05"))  pipeline_report(p, file = "technical-report.html")

title: Moving from ltm, eRm, TAM or irtQ to mirt
text: Give mirtify() code string, path .R file, unquoted inside { }: Three things happen: Model calls become mirt() calls model. ltm::rasch() estimates one common discrimination items, translation adds CONSTRAIN line rather using mirt’s itemtype = "Rasch" (fixes slopes 1 frees latent variance instead). Follow-calls fitted object translated . mirtify() remembers fit came rasch(), factor.scores(fit) becomes fscores() matching method (ltm’s empirical Bayes scores posterior modes, mirt calls MAP). difference gets note, written comment line. Turn notes = FALSE. Code involve packages left . Calls mirt equivalent kept comments, note use instead.
code: mirtify({   library(ltm)   fit <- rasch(LSAT)   summary(fit)   factor.scores(fit)   item.fit(fit) }) #> mirtify: 5 of 5 statements translated from ltm #>  #> # mirtverse loads mirt, so one library() call covers both. #> library(mirtverse) #> # ltm::rasch() estimates one common discrimination for all items; the #> # CONSTRAIN line does the same in mirt. #> # ltm integrates over 21 Gauss-Hermite points and mirt over 61 points, so #> # estimates can differ slightly (usually in the second or third decimal). #> fit_model <- mirt.model("F = 1-5 #>                          CONSTRAIN = (1-5, a1)") #> fit <- mirt(LSAT, fit_model, itemtype = "2PL", SE = TRUE) #> # tidy() lists every parameter with its standard error, on the IRT scale. #> tidy(fit) #> # ltm's empirical Bayes scores are the posterior modes, which mirt calls MAP. #> # Like ltm, full.scores = FALSE returns one row per observed response #> # pattern; drop it to get one score per person. #> fscores(fit, method = "MAP", full.scores = FALSE) #> # Both use Yen's Q1-type chi-square with 10 ability groups, but the groups #> # are formed differently, so the statistics differ a little. fit_stats = #> # "S_X2" is usually preferred in mirt. #> itemfit(fit, fit_stats = "X2")

code: res <- mirtify("fit <- ltm::rasch(LSAT)", run = TRUE) coef(res$env$fit, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items #>                a         b g u #> Item_1 0.7554128 -3.614579 0 1 #> Item_2 0.7554128 -1.322108 0 1 #> Item_3 0.7554128 -0.317661 0 1 #> Item_4 0.7554128 -1.729674 0 1 #> Item_5 0.7554128 -2.779569 0 1

title: Moving from ltm, eRm, TAM or irtQ to mirt
text: eRm estimates Rasch models conditional maximum likelihood (CML), mirt uses marginal maximum likelihood (MML) normal latent trait. Rasch family two give similar item estimates. eRm reports item easiness (minus difficulty) centred sum zero, translated coef() summary() calls convert mirt’s difficulties form. Andersen’s likelihood-ratio test (LRtest()) becomes comparison mirt: model equal item parameters low high score groups one separate parameters. raschdat1 eRm gives LR = 32.5 29 df (p = .30) translation gives 32.8 29 df (p = .29).
code: mirtify({   library(eRm)   fit <- RM(raschdat1)   coef(fit)   pp <- person.parameter(fit)   itemfit(pp)   LRtest(fit)   plotPImap(fit) }) #> mirtify: 7 of 7 statements translated from eRm #>  #> # mirtverse loads mirt, so one library() call covers both. #> library(mirtverse) #> # eRm uses conditional maximum likelihood (CML); mirt uses marginal maximum #> # likelihood with a normal latent trait, so estimates are close but not #> # identical. #> # eRm reports item easiness (beta = -difficulty) centred to sum to zero; #> # coef() and summary() below convert mirt's difficulties to the same form. #> fit <- mirt(raschdat1, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", SE = TRUE) #> # eRm's item easiness is minus the difficulty, centred to sum to zero. #> fit_b <- coef(fit, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "b"] #> -(fit_b - mean(fit_b)) #> # eRm's person parameters are maximum likelihood estimates. For all-correct #> # or all-wrong patterns mirt returns -Inf or Inf where eRm extrapolates; #> # method = "WLE" gives finite values for everyone. #> pp <- fscores(fit, method = "ML", full.scores.SE = TRUE) #> # mirt's infit and outfit mean squares use EAP person estimates while eRm #> # uses ML estimates, so values differ a little. #> itemfit(fit, fit_stats = "infit") #> # Andersen's test compares item parameters across score groups. Here the same #> # comparison is a likelihood-ratio test between a model with equal item #> # parameters in both groups and one with separate parameters. It uses #> # marginal rather than conditional likelihood, so the statistic differs from #> # eRm's. #> fit_score <- rowSums(raschdat1, na.rm = TRUE) #> fit_split <- ifelse(fit_score > median(fit_score), "high", "low") #> fit_free <- multipleGroup(raschdat1, 1, group = fit_split, #>                           itemtype = "Rasch") #> fit_equal <- multipleGroup(raschdat1, 1, group = fit_split, #>                            itemtype = "Rasch", #>                            invariance = c("slopes", "intercepts", "free_means", "free_var")) #> anova(fit_equal, fit_free) #> # gg_wright() draws the person-item map with ggplot2. #> gg_wright(fit)

what: TAM: Q matrices, groups and latent regression
title: Moving from ltm, eRm, TAM or irtQ to mirt
text: tam.mml() tam.mml.2pl() translate used arguments: Q matrix becomes mirt.model() correlated dimensions, group becomes multipleGroup() equal item parameters free group means variances, Y becomes mirt’s latent regression (covdata formula), pweights becomes survey.weights.
code: mirtify("library(TAM)          mod <- tam.mml(resp, Q = Q)          mod2 <- tam.mml.2pl(resp, group = school)          wle <- tam.wle(mod)          wle$WLE.rel          tam.modelfit(mod)          IRT.compareModels(mod, mod2)") #> mirtify: 7 of 7 statements translated from TAM #>  #> # mirtverse loads mirt, so one library() call covers both. #> library(mirtverse) #> # Like TAM, itemtype = "Rasch" fixes the slopes at 1, sets the latent mean to #> # 0 and estimates the latent variance. #> # mirt.model() builds the same between-item structure from TAM's Q matrix, #> # with correlated dimensions. #> # TAM integrates over 21 nodes from -6 to 6 and mirt over 61 points, so #> # estimates can differ slightly. #> mod_model <- mirt.model(Q, COV = upper.tri(diag(ncol(Q)))) #> mod <- mirt(resp, mod_model, itemtype = "Rasch", SE = TRUE) #> # For polytomous items use itemtype = "gpcm", which is what TAM fits for #> # them. #> # As in TAM, the latent variance is fixed at 1 and every item has its own #> # slope. #> # With group, TAM keeps item parameters equal across groups and estimates a #> # mean and variance for each group; multipleGroup() with this invariance does #> # the same. #> mod2 <- multipleGroup(resp, 1, group = school, itemtype = "2PL", #>                       SE = TRUE, #>                       invariance = c("slopes", "intercepts", "free_means", "free_var")) #> # Warm's weighted likelihood estimates, as in tam.wle(). #> wle <- fscores(mod, method = "WLE", full.scores.SE = TRUE) #> empirical_rxx(wle) #> # M2() gives the overall fit test with RMSEA and SRMSR. For TAM's Q3 #> # statistics use residuals(mod, type = "Q3") or gg_q3(mod). #> M2(mod) #> # anova() compares nested mirt models with AIC, BIC and a likelihood-ratio #> # test. #> anova(mod, mod2)

what: irtQ: The scaling constant D and priors
title: Moving from ltm, eRm, TAM or irtQ to mirt
text: irtQ often uses D = 1.702, multiplies every slope. mirt D, slopes equal irtQ’s times 1.702. translated summary() coef() calls divide back. translation also keeps irtQ’s defaults mirt share: 49 quadrature points -6 6, one shared slope 1PLM items, Beta(5, 16) prior guessing parameters.
code: mirtify("library(irtQ)          mod <- est_irt(data = resp, D = 1.702,                         model = c('1PLM', '1PLM', '3PLM', '3PLM', 'GRM'),                         cats = c(2, 2, 2, 2, 4))          summary(mod)          est_score(mod, method = 'WL')          sx2_fit(mod)") #> mirtify: 5 of 5 statements translated from irtQ #>  #> # mirtverse loads mirt, so one library() call covers both. #> library(mirtverse) #> # irtQ's 1PLM items share one estimated slope; the CONSTRAIN line does the #> # same in mirt. #> # irtQ puts a Beta(5, 16) prior on the guessing parameters by default; the #> # PRIOR line does the same in mirt. #> # With guessing parameters the likelihood can have more than one peak, so #> # mirt and irtQ can stop at slightly different estimates. Compare the #> # log-likelihoods if the estimates differ. #> # quadpts and theta_lim use irtQ's quadrature (49 points from -6 to 6). #> # irtQ multiplies the slopes by D = 1.702; mirt does not. mirt's slopes equal #> # irtQ's times 1.702, and coef() and summary() below rescale them. #> mod_model <- mirt.model("F = 1-5 #>                          CONSTRAIN = (1-2, a1) #>                          PRIOR = (3-4, g, expbeta, 5, 16)") #> mod <- mirt(resp, mod_model, #>             itemtype = c(rep("2PL", 2), rep("3PL", 2), "graded"), #>             quadpts = 49, theta_lim = c(-6, 6), SE = TRUE) #> mod_pars <- coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items #> mod_pars[, "a"] <- mod_pars[, "a"] / 1.702  # irtQ's slopes include D = 1.702 #> mod_pars #> fscores(mod, method = "WLE", full.scores.SE = TRUE) #> # Orlando and Thissen's S-X2, as in irtQ. #> itemfit(mod, fit_stats = "S_X2")

title: Moving from ltm, eRm, TAM or irtQ to mirt
text: package tests fit model original package translated mirt code, compare estimates. largest absolute differences: small differences come number quadrature points (ltm uses 21 TAM 21, mirt 61) convergence tolerances. Two cases differ , notes say : Polytomous Rasch models eRm (PCM()): eRm centres item parameters mirt centres persons, compare thresholds subtracting mean. 3PL models guessing prior irtQ: likelihood can one peak, two packages may stop slightly different estimates. Compare log-likelihoods estimates differ.

text: Several rules available. default "residual" rule flags response much faster expected person item. normative threshold rules "nt10", "nt15" "nt20" flag responses faster 10%, 15% 20% item’s mean time, threshold capped 10 seconds (Wise & Ma, 2012). code: # \donttest{ set.seed(1) a <- matrix(rlnorm(8, 0.2, 0.3)); d <- matrix(rnorm(8)) d2 <- d; d2[1] <- d2[1] - 1 data <- rbind(simdata(a, d, 400, itemtype = "2PL"),               simdata(a, d2, 400, itemtype = "2PL")) gender <- rep(c("F", "M"), each = 400) res <- dif(data, group = gender) res #> DIF analysis: F (reference) vs M; 8 items tested #> Likelihood-ratio tests freeing a1, d; BH-adjusted p < 0.05 flags DIF #>  #>    item     X2 df p.value p.adjusted flag    esd  uesd converged #>  Item_1 47.375  2  < .001     < .001  DIF -0.220 0.220      TRUE #>  Item_2  2.735  2    .255       .529      -0.009 0.059      TRUE #>  Item_3  1.804  2    .406       .529       0.041 0.041      TRUE #>  Item_4  2.441  2    .295       .529       0.037 0.044      TRUE #>  Item_5  1.885  2    .390       .529       0.039 0.040      TRUE #>  Item_6  0.452  2    .798       .798      -0.016 0.016      TRUE #>  Item_7  1.542  2    .463       .529      -0.023 0.043      TRUE #>  Item_8  3.739  2    .154       .529       0.059 0.059      TRUE gg_dif(res)  interpret(res) #> DIF overview #> ------------ #> * Items were tested for DIF between F and M, with F as the reference group (n #>   = 400 F, n = 400 M).  #> * Each item's parameters (a1, d) were freed in turn and compared with a model #>   holding them equal across groups (likelihood-ratio test, BH-adjusted p < #>   0.05).  #> * On the common scale, the M group's mean ability is 0.09 SD below the F #>   group's, and its SD is 1.23.  #>  #> DIF items #> --------- #> * 1 of 8 items show DIF: Item_1 (expected score difference -0.220, favours F; #>   p < .001).  #> * Statistical DIF is not proof of bias: ask content experts whether these #>   items measure something other than the intended ability for one group #>   before removing or revising them.  #>  # }

title: Plain-language interpretation of IRT results — interpret.mv_dif
text: Rules thumb used: RMSEA (M2/C2): <= .05 close, <= .08 reasonable, <= .10 mediocre, otherwise poor. Marginal reliability: >= .90 excellent, >= .80 good, >= .70 acceptable. Discrimination: < 0.5 low, > 4 suspiciously high; location beyond +/- 3 extreme; guessing > .30 high; S-X2 p < alpha misfit. Local dependence: Q3 0.2 average Q3. Person fit: Zh < -1.96 flags aberrant response patterns.

title: Translate ltm, eRm, TAM and irtQ code into mirt code — mirtify
code: mirtify("library(ltm)          fit <- rasch(LSAT)          summary(fit)          factor.scores(fit)") #> mirtify: 4 of 4 statements translated from ltm #>  #> # mirtverse loads mirt, so one library() call covers both. #> library(mirtverse) #> # ltm::rasch() estimates one common discrimination for all items; the #> # CONSTRAIN line does the same in mirt. #> # ltm integrates over 21 Gauss-Hermite points and mirt over 61 points, so #> # estimates can differ slightly (usually in the second or third decimal). #> fit_model <- mirt.model(sprintf("F = 1-%1$d #>                                  CONSTRAIN = (1-%1$d, a1)", ncol(LSAT))) #> fit <- mirt(LSAT, fit_model, itemtype = "2PL", SE = TRUE) #> # tidy() lists every parameter with its standard error, on the IRT scale. #> tidy(fit) #> # ltm's empirical Bayes scores are the posterior modes, which mirt calls MAP. #> # Like ltm, full.scores = FALSE returns one row per observed response #> # pattern; drop it to get one score per person. #> fscores(fit, method = "MAP", full.scores = FALSE)  # Unquoted code works too mirtify({   library(eRm)   fit <- RM(raschdat1)   pp <- person.parameter(fit)   itemfit(pp)   LRtest(fit) }) #> mirtify: 5 of 5 statements translated from eRm #>  #> # mirtverse loads mirt, so one library() call covers both. #> library(mirtverse) #> # eRm uses conditional maximum likelihood (CML); mirt uses marginal maximum #> # likelihood with a normal latent trait, so estimates are close but not #> # identical. #> # eRm reports item easiness (beta = -difficulty) centred to sum to zero; #> # coef() and summary() below convert mirt's difficulties to the same form. #> fit <- mirt(raschdat1, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", SE = TRUE) #> # eRm's person parameters are maximum likelihood estimates. For all-correct #> # or all-wrong patterns mirt returns -Inf or Inf where eRm extrapolates; #> # method = "WLE" gives finite values for everyone. #> pp <- fscores(fit, method = "ML", full.scores.SE = TRUE) #> # mirt's infit and outfit mean squares use EAP person estimates while eRm #> # uses ML estimates, so values differ a little. #> itemfit(fit, fit_stats = "infit") #> # Andersen's test compares item parameters across score groups. Here the same #> # comparison is a likelihood-ratio test between a model with equal item #> # parameters in both groups and one with separate parameters. It uses #> # marginal rather than conditional likelihood, so the statistic differs from #> # eRm's. #> fit_score <- rowSums(raschdat1, na.rm = TRUE) #> fit_split <- ifelse(fit_score > median(fit_score), "high", "low") #> fit_free <- multipleGroup(raschdat1, 1, group = fit_split, #>                           itemtype = "Rasch") #> fit_equal <- multipleGroup(raschdat1, 1, group = fit_split, #>                            itemtype = "Rasch", #>                            invariance = c("slopes", "intercepts", "free_means", "free_var")) #> anova(fit_equal, fit_free)  mirtify("mod <- irtQ::est_irt(data = resp, D = 1.702, model = '3PLM')") #> mirtify: 1 of 1 statements translated from irtQ #>  #> library(mirtverse) #> # irtQ puts a Beta(5, 16) prior on the guessing parameters by default; the #> # PRIOR line does the same in mirt. #> # With guessing parameters the likelihood can have more than one peak, so #> # mirt and irtQ can stop at slightly different estimates. Compare the #> # log-likelihoods if the estimates differ. #> # quadpts and theta_lim use irtQ's quadrature (49 points from -6 to 6). #> # irtQ multiplies the slopes by D = 1.702; mirt does not. mirt's slopes equal #> # irtQ's times 1.702, and coef() and summary() below rescale them. #> mod_model <- mirt.model(sprintf("F = 1-%1$d #>                                  PRIOR = (1-%1$d, g, expbeta, 5, 16)", ncol(resp))) #> mod <- mirt(resp, mod_model, itemtype = "3PL", quadpts = 49, #>             theta_lim = c(-6, 6), SE = TRUE)

Flags three levels. info flags shown awareness. review flags point something psychometrician look . block flags point problems make later stages unsafe, model converge item large DIF. default flags warn: Every stage runs, warning lists open flags moving past. strict = TRUE, stage refuses run earlier stage open review flags (record decision acknowledge()) open block flags (fix problem, example drop_items(), record reason override()). title: Interactive IRT teaching labs — run_lab
text: mirtverse ships interactive learnr tutorials measurement courses. Students work realistic testing scenario live R exercises make decisions analyst make, getting feedback one. Labs 1 2 share one storyline, certification board's 32-item exam (certexam). Labs 3 10 : provincial numeracy test (numeracy), licensure exam two forms (linking), placement test's item bank (catbank), rater-scored science tasks (openended), written science explanations (essays), text numeracy items (itemtext), field test generated items (aigfield) AI-scored science test (aiscored).

title: Interactive IRT teaching labs — run_lab
text: "model-choice" (Lab 1): Score responses, screen items, check dimensionality, compare Rasch, 2PL 3PL models, check item fit local dependence, commit model board can defend. "decisions" (Lab 2): Read item parameters, check precision pass mark, choose scoring method, estimate classification accuracy, test DIF English French candidates, write memo, compare results truth behind data. "fairness" (Lab 3): numeracy test biased English language learners? Separate impact DIF, run Mantel-Haenszel IRT likelihood-ratio DIF tests, purify anchor, judge much DIF matters students' scores plan content review. "linking" (Lab 4): licensure exam's pass rate jumped new form. Calibrate forms, link common items, catch drifted anchor, compare separate concurrent calibration, carry pass mark IRT true-score equating. "cat-design" (Lab 5): computerized adaptive test replace 40-item placement test? Inspect item bank, run CAT hand, simulate students, choose stopping rule, exposure control content balancing. "open-ended" (Lab 6): rubric scores science assessment trustworthy? Check rater agreement, find severe inconsistent rater, resolve final scores, fit polytomous IRT models, collapse categories work, decide whether automated scoring engine can replace human reader. "auto-scoring" (Lab 7): Can automated scoring engine score written science explanations ? Train engine train_scorer(), judge new students agreement_report(), check English language learners, find drives difference, choose engine's role. "item-text" (Lab 8): Can item difficulty predicted text field testing? Describe items item_features(), find near-duplicates miskeyed items, compare LLTM lasso random forest predict_difficulty(), catch leaky feature, hold whole item models, decide predictions can replace. "aig" (Lab 9): Can family mean replace field test generated item? Write item model item_model() fix constraints, calibrate field test 60 isomorphs, find families isomorphic calibrate_families() , test family means held-items. "ai-audit" (Lab 10): Can scores AI-scored test released? Audit engine ai_audit(): Agreement human raters, bias English language learners, drift engine update DIF test scored; draft validity argument validity_argument() decide scores report. run_lab() opens lab browser (RStudio Viewer). labs also appear RStudio's Tutorial pane mirtverse learnr installed. Progress saved browser, students can stop come back later.

Overall bias: 4 tested, flagged CR3 [SMD +0.29]. #>   To do: Resolve the flags, then rerun the audit before the scores are #>     used. #>  #> Generalization [NEEDS EVIDENCE] #>   Claim: Scores would be the same on another occasion, form, rater or #>     engine version, so they mean the same across administrations. #>   Threats: An engine update, a new prompt or a change in the population #>     shifts machine scores; agreement holds in one year only. #>   Evidence: None yet. #>   To do: Check drift across administrations and engine versions with #>     ai_audit(period = ). #>  #> Extrapolation [THREATENED] #>   Claim: Scores reflect Grade 8 science, and do so equally for all #>     groups of Grade 8 students. #>   Threats: Features unrelated to the construct, such as language #>     proficiency, lower machine scores for some groups; DIF on AI-scored #>     items. #>   Evidence: Subgroup agreement: 8 tested, flagged CR3, ELL [QWK 0.68]; #>     CR4, Fluent [QWK 0.67]; CR4, ELL [QWK 0.60]. Differential scoring: #>     4 tested, flagged CR2, ELL [gap -0.23 SD, SE 0.07]. #>   To do: Resolve the flags, then rerun the audit before the scores are #>     used. Not checked yet: DIF. #>  #> Decision [NEEDS EVIDENCE] #>   Claim: Using the scores for school accountability is appropriate, #>     with the human oversight, disclosure and appeals the use requires. #>   Threats: Machine scores are used without human review where stakes #>     are high; test takers are not told how they were scored; errors #>     cannot be appealed. #>   Evidence: None yet. #>   To do: Document human review of flagged and low-confidence responses, #>     disclosure to test takers, and an appeals process. No audit can #>     supply this evidence. #>  cat(format(va, "markdown")) #> The argument for using Grade 8 science scores for school accountability, with automated scoring of constructed responses, by the four inferences of the argument-based approach (Kane, 2013). #>  #> ### Scoring (threatened) #>  #> - **Claim:** Scores from automated scoring of constructed responses follow the scoring rubric as trained human raters apply it. #> - **Threats:** The engine rewards surface features (length, vocabulary, spelling) rather than the ideas in the rubric; human scores used to train or check it are unreliable. #> - **Evidence:** Human agreement: 4 tested, flagged CR4 [human QWK 0.63]. Machine agreement: 4 tested, flagged CR4 [QWK 0.66, human QWK 0.63]. Overall bias: 4 tested, flagged CR3 [SMD +0.29]. #> - **To do:** Resolve the flags, then rerun the audit before the scores are used. #>  #> ### Generalization (needs evidence) #>  #> - **Claim:** Scores would be the same on another occasion, form, rater or engine version, so they mean the same across administrations. #> - **Threats:** An engine update, a new prompt or a change in the population shifts machine scores; agreement holds in one year only. #> - **Evidence:** None yet. #> - **To do:** Check drift across administrations and engine versions with ai_audit(period = ). #>  #> ### Extrapolation (threatened) #>  #> - **Claim:** Scores reflect Grade 8 science, and do so equally for all groups of Grade 8 students. #> - **Threats:** Features unrelated to the construct, such as language proficiency, lower machine scores for some groups; DIF on AI-scored items. #> - **Evidence:** Subgroup agreement: 8 tested, flagged CR3, ELL [QWK 0.68]; CR4, Fluent [QWK 0.67]; CR4, ELL [QWK 0.60]. Differential scoring: 4 tested, flagged CR2, ELL [gap -0.23 SD, SE 0.07]. #> - **To do:** Resolve the flags, then rerun the audit before the scores are used. Not checked yet: DIF. #>  #> ### Decision (needs evidence) #>  #> - **Claim:** Using the scores for school accountability is appropriate, with the human oversight, disclosure and appeals the use requires. #> - **Threats:** Machine scores are used without human review where stakes are high; test takers are not told how they were scored; errors cannot be appealed. #> - **Evidence:** None yet. #> - **To do:** Document human review of flagged and low-confidence responses, disclosure to test takers, and an appeals process. No audit can supply this evidence.
